title: At global BOLD peaks, thalamus and brainstem voxels near cerebrospinal fluid were later than voxels far from it, and no deep tissue led the cortex, in 61 held-out OpenNeuro task and rest studies
abstract:
In fMRI, thalamus and brainstem voxels that touch cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rise about 1 s later than voxels of the same structures far from CSF, at the moments when the whole cortex rises together. This matters because the timing of deep regions at these global peaks is used as a sign of arousal centres; at standard fMRI resolution much of it is set by where a voxel lies relative to CSF and the veins in CSF spaces, and tissue far from CSF did not lead the cortex.

We used ReadyNeuro: minimally preprocessed BOLD fMRI from OpenNeuro, one person per study, with each person's own 1 mm brain segmentation. Global peaks are peaks of the mean cortical signal (about one per minute). For each voxel of the thalamus, brainstem and ventral diencephalon we averaged the signal around the peaks and measured its phase: how far it is behind (+) or ahead of (-) the cortex (1 degree is about 0.06 s). We compared voxels within 2 mm of CSF with voxels more than 4 mm from CSF in the same image slices. We fixed the study lists before reading data, found the pattern in 11 discovery studies, pre-registered the tests, confirmed them in 41 task-fMRI studies, and then in 20 further studies with rest runs only.

Near voxels were later than far voxels by a median of 20.7 degrees (95% CI 17.0 to 25.3) in 41 of 41 task studies and by 24.3 degrees in 20 of 20 rest studies (thalamus 17 and 21 degrees, brainstem 28 and 26 degrees; ventral diencephalon no difference). In full-run cross-correlation this was 1.2 s. The phase fell step by step with distance to CSF. Far from CSF no structure led the cortex at any distance threshold: in task runs far thalamus was +0.1 degrees (CI -2.5 to 3.9) against cortex far from CSF; at rest it was about 0.8 s later. The rule held across repetition times, slice orders, white-matter content, tSNR matching and head motion. A simple tissue-CSF mixture did not fit the size of the effect; veins in CSF spaces or a vascular delay next to CSF fit better. At literature arousal sites (dorsal midline thalamus, nucleus basalis, substantia nigra) all voxels rose with the cortex, and the near-CSF voxels were the late ones. Periventricular lateness was known from lag maps; new are the distance rule inside deep grey matter, its presence in every study, and the bound on leads far from CSF.

Limits: 2 mm voxels, rigid alignment, no distortion correction; one person per study; veins and CSF not separated; small nuclei below the resolution.

display.caption: Event-locked BOLD around peaks of the cortical global signal (time 0), mean over studies with 95% CI. Rows: discovery (11 studies, mostly task), confirmation (41 task studies), rest extension (20 studies, rest runs only). Orange: deep grey-matter voxels within 2 mm of CSF; blue: more than 4 mm from CSF; dashed grey: cortex. Right column: lateral-ventricle atrium and white matter near and far from CSF.

Left: phase of deep grey matter (thalamus, brainstem, ventral diencephalon) relative to the cortex at global peaks, by distance to the nearest CSF voxel in the person's own 1 mm segmentation (positive = later). Thin lines: studies; dots: medians. Right: per-study slice-matched difference between near (<= 2 mm) and far (> 4 mm) voxels; black bars: medians. Every study of all three sets is above zero.

Group phase of deep-brain voxels at global cortical peaks (52 studies of the discovery and confirmation sets, rigid MNI alignment, voxels with coupling amplitude above 0.08). Red: later than the cortex; blue: earlier. A late rim follows the ventricle walls and cisterns; the third ventricle is early; the thalamic interior is in phase.
